The Chevron Opinion
In 1984, the Court addressed the topic of judicial deference in an 
opinion that would come to define an era—Chevron, U.S.A., Inc. v. Natural 
Resources Defense Council, Inc., 4,^1 U.S. 837 (1984). In an opinion 
authored by Justice Stevens, the Court appeared to embrace a two-part 
test for assessing deference to agency statutory construction. The case 
came to characterize a particular approach to judicial review of agency 
statutory interpretations—Chevron deference. But from the start, the 
precise meaning of the Chevron opinion was disputed.
Chevron concerned the proper construction of the Clean Air Act 
Amendments of 1977. In that statute. Congress had required certain 
“nonattainment” States—^those that had not achieved the national air 
quality standards set by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)—to 
establish permit programs regulating “new or modified major stationary 
sources” of air pollution. A permit could not be issued for a new or modified 
major stationary source without meeting several stringent conditions.
On October 14, 1981, the EPA promulgated a regulation to implement 
the permit requirement, allowing a State to adopt a plantwide definition of 
the term “stationary source.” Specifically, the regulation defined a 
“[b]uilding, structure, facility, or installation” as including “all of the 
pollutant-emitting activities which belong to the same industrial grouping, 
are located on one or more contiguous or adjacent properties, and are under 
the control of the same person (or persons under common control) except 
the activities of any vessel.” This definition permitted an existing plant 
containing several pollution-emitting devices to install or modify a piece of 
equipment without meeting the permit conditions, so long as the alteration 
did not increase the plant’s total emissions. The question presented in the 
Chevron litigation was whether EPA’s regulation allowing States “to treat 
all of the pollution-emitting devices within the same industrial grouping as 
though they were encased within a single ‘bubble’ ” lawfully interpreted 
the term “stationary source.”
In an opinion by then-Judge (later Justice) Ruth Bader Ginsburg, the 
D.C. Circuit set aside the regulation. Relying on earlier D.C. Circuit 
precedent. Judge Ginsburg held that the bubble concept could not be 
applied to these cases.
The Supreme Court reversed. It began its analysis by asserting that 
“[t]he basic legal error of the Court of Appeals was to adopt a static judicial 
definition of the term ‘stationary source’ when it had decided that Congress 
itself had not commanded that definition.” Then, in passages that have 
often been quoted, the Court announced:
